entities.name: Prior ODMR work distinguished two optical-spin-interface mechanisms: established ODMR systems such as NV centers in diamond, SiC defects, and VB defects in hBN
entities.description: Prior ODMR work distinguished two optical-spin-interface mechanisms: established ODMR systems such as NV centers in diamond, SiC defects, and VB defects in hBN were understood via spin-dependent intersystem crossing, whereas more recent S=1/2-like ODMR reports in hBN, GaN, and β-GeS2 were attributed instead to spin-dependent charge transfer between defect pairs; in hBN, such spin-pair ODMR was noted to be ubiquitous over a wide range of laser excitation wavelengths.
entities.evidence_span: These systems, including the NV defect in diamond, rely on spin-dependent intersys- tem crossings between the ground and excited states [11].

evidence_spans: These systems, including the NV defect in diamond, rely on spin-dependent intersys- tem crossings between the ground and excited states [11].

More recently, a series of observations in hBN [12–19], gallium nitride (GaN) [20], and β-germanium disulphide (β-GeS2) [21, 22] have identified an ODMR signature akin to a S = 1/2 resonance, which is generally con- sidered to be inconsistent with the intersystem cross- ing optical-spin interface and may instead be better ex- plained by spin dependent charge transfer between defect pairs [18].
A characteristic feature for the optical spin defect pairs in hBN is the ubiquity of the ODMR signal under a wide range of different wavelengths of laser excitation [33].
